messages.author: 5140016d70f6ba82
messages.subject: Re: variance-covariance
parts:
Sure. The following is off the top of my head so you should work
through the delta method variances and covariances. I believe the
covariance term for a line transect example would be
n_i*n_j*var(f(0))/(L_i*L_j) assuming that the lines were randomly
selected so there is no covariance in the encounter rate between lines.
The diagonal variances are f(0)*f(0)*var(n_i/L_i) and you'll have to get
creative there because there is no empirical way of estimating the
variance from a single line. You can probably take the combined
L^2*var(n/L)/n as an estimate of b and then use b*n_i/L_i^2 as the
estimate of the variance of the encounter rate for each line. If you
are creating the v-c matrix for density then the above is missing
relevant constant terms and any aspect of average group size but that
should get you started in the right direction. Steve do we have this
anywhere in the books?

--jeff

messages.subject: Re: variance-covariance
parts:
> > should get you started in the right direction. Steve do we have this
> > anywhere in the books?

No - which is a pity! The closest we get is p85 of the 2001 introductory
book, showing how to get the var of a difference in density estimates,
when f^(0) is common to the 2 estimates. There is a more complicated
example in section 8.5.

Steve
